q: After this 625 battle near a mountain north of Medina, the Muslims suffered losses when archers left their posts and Muhammad was wounded. Hamza was killed. For 10 points, name this battle that followed Badr.

This 636 battle on a river in Syria saw Khalid ibn al-Walid's Muslim army defeat the Byzantines of Heraclius. It opened the way to the conquest of Syria. For 10 points, name this battle named for a tributary of the Jordan.

In 628 Muhammad signed this treaty with the Quraysh, allowing Muslims to make pilgrimage the following year and promising a ten-year truce. Some of his followers considered it humiliating, but the Quran calls it a clear victory. For 10 points, name this treaty.

This dynasty claimed descent from Fatima and ruled in Tunisia and Egypt, founding Cairo in 969 and the al-Azhar mosque. It belonged to the Ismaili branch of Shia Islam. For 10 points, name this caliphate.

This empire, founded by Osman, captured Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II. At its height under Suleiman it spread across the Balkans, Anatolia, and Arab lands. For 10 points, name this empire whose sultans were also caliphs.

This dynasty, founded by Ismail I in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran. It built a capital at Isfahan under Shah Abbas. For 10 points, name this dynasty, rivals of the Ottomans.

This eighteenth-century reformer from the Najd preached strict monotheism and attacked tomb veneration. He allied with Muhammad ibn Saud in 1744. For 10 points, name this figure whose followers are called Wahhabis.
This Hanbali jurist, born in Harran in 1263, wrote fatwas against the Mongols and the excesses of Sufism. His ideas influenced later reformers. For 10 points, name this scholar of Damascus.

This Sunni school of law, the oldest and most widely followed, was founded by a scholar of Kufa who stressed analogy and reason. It dominated the Ottoman Empire and is followed in Turkey and South Asia. For 10 points, name this school, named for Abu Hanifa.
This largest Shia branch holds that the line of imams ended with the twelfth, who is in hiding. Iran and Iraq are home to most of its followers. For 10 points, name this branch, also called Imamiyya.
This Shia branch split from the Twelvers over the succession of Ismail, son of Jafar al-Sadiq. The Aga Khan leads one group, the Nizari. For 10 points, name this branch, also called the Seveners.

Shia Muslims believe that this figure, the twelfth imam, entered a state of occultation in the ninth century. He is expected to return and bring justice. For 10 points, give this title, also used in Sunni belief for a messianic deliverer.

This theological school, popular under the early Abbasids, held that the Quran was created and that human reason can know good and evil. It was favored by al-Mamun during the Mihna. For 10 points, name this rationalist school.

This Arabic word, meaning "oneness," names the central doctrine of Islam: that God is one and has no partners. Surah 112, al-Ikhlas, is regarded as a summary of it. Violating it is the sin of shirk. For 10 points, give this term.

This independent legal effort, from a root meaning "to strive," involves a scholar using reasoning to reach a ruling. Traditional scholars say its "gate" was closed, but modernists reject that. For 10 points, name this concept.

This former Ethiopian slave, a companion of Muhammad, became the first muezzin. According to tradition he was tortured in Mecca, with a heavy rock laid on his chest in the heat, for refusing to renounce his faith. He was freed by Abu Bakr and was known for his beautiful voice. For 10 points, name this man.

This building is known for its horseshoe arches and a forest of columns in a city in Andalusia. It was begun by Abd al-Rahman I and later turned into a cathedral. For 10 points, name this Andalusian mosque-cathedral.

This Sufi mystic of Baghdad, executed in 922, proclaimed "I am the Truth." He was accused of heresy and crucified. He studied under Junayd, wrote the Kitab al-Tawasin, and traveled widely before his trial. For 10 points, name this man.
This Andalusian mystic, called "the greatest master," wrote the Meccan Revelations. His doctrine of the unity of being influenced later Sufis. For 10 points, name this author of Bezels of Wisdom.
This wife of Muhammad, daughter of Abu Bakr, was said to have been nine at her marriage. She narrated many hadith and led forces at the Battle of the Camel in 656. For 10 points, name this woman.
This religious opinion, issued by a mufti, is a nonbinding ruling on a question of Islamic law. A famous example was issued against Salman Rushdie in 1989. For 10 points, give this term.

parts: Which philosopher is known in Latin as Avicenna?
Which philosopher of Baghdad, called the "philosopher of the Arabs," wrote on the intellect and arithmetic?
Which tenth-century philosopher, called the "Second Teacher," wrote The Virtuous City?

q: This agreement of 622 or 623, drawn up by Muhammad soon after the Hijra, regulated relations among Muslims, Jews, and pagan tribes of a certain city. It declared the signatories one community, or ummah, and set rules for blood money and mutual defense. It is regarded as an early written constitution. For 10 points, name this document, named for its city.

This second-century Indian philosopher wrote the Mulamadhyamakakarika, which argues that all phenomena lack inherent existence. He founded the Madhyamaka school and is often called the "second Buddha" in Tibet. For 10 points, name this Mahayana thinker whose name contains the word for serpent beings.

This Buddhist concept, often translated as "emptiness," holds that things have no independent essence. The Heart Sutra states that form is this and this is form. For 10 points, give this Sanskrit term central to Madhyamaka.

This collection of early Buddhist scriptures, whose name means "Three Baskets," is divided into the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma. The Theravada school preserves it in Pali. For 10 points, name this canon.

This Mahayana scripture, translated into Chinese by Kumarajiva, teaches that all beings can attain Buddhahood. It contains parables such as the burning house. Nichiren Buddhists chant its title. For 10 points, name this sutra.

This thirteenth-century Japanese monk taught that the Lotus Sutra alone offered salvation. He chanted "Namu Myoho Renge Kyo" and predicted a Mongol invasion. For 10 points, name this founder of a Buddhist school named for him.

This Japanese Pure Land teacher, a disciple of Honen, taught that faith in Amida Buddha alone brings rebirth in the Pure Land. He married and founded the Jodo Shinshu tradition. For 10 points, name this monk.
This eighth-century Indian tantric master is said to have subdued demons and founded the first monastery at Samye in Tibet. Tibetans call him Guru Rinpoche. For 10 points, name this man.

This fourteenth-century Tibetan reformer founded the Gelug school and Ganden Monastery. He wrote the Lamrim Chenmo, a graded path to enlightenment. For 10 points, name this teacher whose school produced the Dalai Lamas.

This Tibetan text, often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead, describes the intermediate state between death and rebirth. It is read aloud to the dying. For 10 points, give this title, from a word for the "liberation through hearing."
This semi-legendary Indian monk is said to have arrived in China around 500 and sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin. He is credited with founding Chan Buddhism. For 10 points, name this man.

This seventh-century Chinese monk traveled to India, studied at Nalanda, and returned with hundreds of Sanskrit texts. His journey was the basis of the novel Journey to the West. For 10 points, name this pilgrim.
This Indian emperor's Rock Edicts promote dhamma after the carnage of the Kalinga war. He sponsored the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra. For 10 points, name this Mauryan ruler.
This Hindu philosophical school, developed by Shankara, teaches non-dualism: Brahman alone is real and the world is illusion. For 10 points, name this school of Vedanta, from Sanskrit for "not two."

This eleventh-century South Indian philosopher taught that Brahman is a personal God with the world and souls as his body. He founded the Vishishtadvaita school. For 10 points, name this Vaishnava theologian.

This Indian sage compiled aphorisms on the eight limbs of yoga, including yama, niyama, asana, and samadhi. The text is organized in four chapters, or padas, and defines yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind. For 10 points, name this author of the Yoga Sutras.

This Hindu festival, held every twelve years in rotation at four sites including Prayagraj and Haridwar, draws millions who bathe at river confluences. For 10 points, name this gathering named for a pot.
This Hindu festival lasts nine nights and honors the goddess in forms such as Durga. It ends with Dussehra, which celebrates the victory of Rama over Ravana. For 10 points, name this festival.

This black-skinned Hindu goddess is shown with a garland of skulls, a protruding tongue, and standing on Shiva. She is associated with time and destruction and worshipped in Kolkata. For 10 points, name this form of the Mother Goddess.

This Bengali mystic, a priest at Dakshineswar, taught that all religions lead to God. He worshipped the goddess Kali and, according to his biographers, spent time practicing Islam and Christian devotion. His disciple Vivekananda spread his message in the West. For 10 points, name this holy man.

This Hindu monk addressed the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago, beginning "Sisters and brothers of America." He founded the Ramakrishna Mission. For 10 points, name this disciple of Ramakrishna.

This Chinese philosopher's namesake book includes the story of the butterfly dream and the cook who carves oxen. He argued for spontaneity and relativity of viewpoints. For 10 points, name this Daoist, second to Laozi.

This Confucian philosopher argued that human nature is good and compared its tendencies to sprouts. He lived in the fourth century BCE and told of a mother who moved three times to educate him. For 10 points, name this "second sage."

This Confucian argued that human nature is bad and must be shaped by ritual and education. His students included the Legalists Han Fei and Li Si. For 10 points, name this third-century BCE philosopher.

This Song dynasty scholar synthesized Confucian ideas with metaphysics, emphasizing li and qi and the Four Books. His commentaries became the basis of civil service exams. For 10 points, name this Neo-Confucian.

This ancient Chinese divination text consists of sixty-four hexagrams made of broken and unbroken lines. Confucian tradition adds commentaries called the Ten Wings. For 10 points, name this "Book of Changes."

This Japanese collection of 712, compiled by Ō no Yasumaro, tells the creation of the islands by Izanagi and Izanami. It is the oldest surviving Shinto-related chronicle. For 10 points, name this book.

This sun goddess of Shinto hid in a cave, plunging the world into darkness, until she was lured out by a dance and a mirror. The imperial family claims descent from her. For 10 points, name this kami.

This Jain sect's monks go without clothes, while the other main sect wears white robes. In their tradition, Mahavira never married and women cannot attain liberation directly. Its name means "sky-clad." For 10 points, name this group, contrasted with the Svetambara.

This fifth Sikh guru compiled the Adi Granth and built the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar. According to tradition he invited the Muslim saint Mian Mir to lay the temple's foundation. He was executed by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. For 10 points, name this first Sikh martyr.

Which Japanese school stresses chanting to Amida?

q: This collection of 423 verses in the Pali Canon, attributed to the Buddha, begins "Mind is the forerunner of all things." It is organized in twenty-six chapters including those on the mind, the thousands, and the monk. It is among the most widely read and translated Buddhist texts. For 10 points, name this anthology.

This pharaoh, born Amenhotep IV, moved the capital to Amarna and promoted the worship of the sun disk. He closed temples of Amun and left behind the Great Hymn to the sun. Nefertiti was his queen. For 10 points, name this Eighteenth Dynasty ruler, father of Tutankhamun.

This sun disk, depicted with rays ending in hands, was the sole god promoted by a pharaoh who built a capital at Akhetaten. For 10 points, name this deity, whose worship replaced the cult of Amun for a time.

This medieval dualist movement in southern France, centered on Albi and Toulouse, taught that the material world was evil. Its adherents, the "perfecti," were persecuted in a crusade launched by Innocent III in 1209. For 10 points, name this heresy, also called Albigensian.

This twelfth-century merchant of Lyon gave away his wealth to preach in poverty and had his teachings condemned in 1184. His followers, who rejected purgatory, later joined the Protestant churches. For 10 points, name this namesake of a movement.

This Czech priest of Prague, influenced by Wycliffe, preached in the Bethlehem Chapel and was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415. His followers started the Hussite Wars. For 10 points, name this reformer.

This small religious community, still living at Mount Gerizim near Nablus, accepts only its own version of the Torah. It considers itself the true Israel and offers Passover sacrifices. For 10 points, name this group.

This Gnostic-influenced group of southern Iraq and Iran reveres John the Baptist and uses baptism in flowing water. Their scripture is the Ginza Rabba, written in a dialect of Aramaic. For 10 points, name this group.

This seventeenth-century Jewish mystic from Smyrna declared himself the Messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam under pressure from the Ottoman sultan. For 10 points, name this man whose followers were called Sabbateans.

This Chinese man, who failed the civil service exam, claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus. He led a rebellion from 1850 and founded the Heavenly Kingdom in Nanjing. For 10 points, name this leader of the Taiping.

This Swedish scientist wrote Heaven and Hell after a series of visions in 1745. Followers who founded the New Church believed in correspondences between spiritual and natural worlds. For 10 points, name this man.

This celibate communal sect, formally the United Society of Believers, was led in America by Ann Lee. It is known for ecstatic dancing, simple furniture, and a hymn "Simple Gifts." For 10 points, name this group.
This Vermont preacher founded a community in New York in 1848 based on "complex marriage" and communal living. It later made silverware. For 10 points, name this man who founded the Oneida Community.
This Russian-born cofounder of the Theosophical Society wrote Isis Unveiled and The Secret Doctrine. She claimed contact with hidden Masters in Tibet. For 10 points, name this woman.

These sisters of Hydesville, New York, claimed in 1848 to communicate with a spirit through knocking sounds. Their claims started the Spiritualist movement. For 10 points, give this surname of the sisters.

This Native American Church uses a cactus containing mescaline as a sacrament. Its buttons are chewed or brewed into tea, and the church was incorporated in Oklahoma in 1918. Its meetings are held in a tipi and last all night. For 10 points, name the plant used.

This Plains ceremony, held in the summer and involving fasting and dancing around a central pole, is sometimes accompanied by piercing. The Lakota call it wiwang wacipi. For 10 points, name this ritual.

This text of the K'iche' Maya recounts the creation and the adventures of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, in the underworld Xibalba. It was transcribed in the Latin alphabet in the sixteenth century and copied by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximenez. For 10 points, name this book.

This Inca sun god was worshipped at the Coricancha in Cusco. His temple was said to be lined with sheets of gold, and a festival at the June solstice honored him. The Inca emperor claimed descent from him. For 10 points, name this deity.
This indigenous religion of Tibet, older than Buddhism, has priests who perform funerals and rituals. Its followers now often use Buddhist-like monasteries. For 10 points, name this religion.
This sky god worshipped by Turks and Mongols was called Eternal Blue Sky. The Khans claimed his mandate. For 10 points, name this deity whose religion was practiced by Genghis Khan's people.

This divination system of the Yoruba uses a palm nut tray and sixteen principal figures called odu. The deity Orunmila presides over it, and Ile-Ife in Nigeria is regarded as its center. Its priests are called babalawo. For 10 points, name this system.
This Afro-Brazilian religion, with houses called terreiros, honors orixas such as Oxala and Iemanja. It developed in Bahia among Yoruba-descended enslaved people. For 10 points, name this religion.

This religion of Lebanon, Syria, and Israel developed from Ismaili Shia Islam in the eleventh century. It venerates the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim and does not accept converts. For 10 points, name this group.
This Vietnamese religion founded in 1926 blends Buddhism, Confucianism, Christianity, and spiritism. Its Holy See is in Tay Ninh, and its symbol is an eye. For 10 points, name this religion.
This Japanese new religion, founded by Nakayama Miki in 1838, centers on a pillar called Jiba in a town near Nara. Followers believe in God the Parent. For 10 points, name this religion.

This English civil servant published Witchcraft Today in 1954 and helped found modern Wicca. He wrote High Magic's Aid and claimed initiation by a woman named Dorothy Clutterbuck. He claimed to be initiated into a New Forest coven. For 10 points, name this man.
This 1961 merger of two American denominations created a liberal religion with no creed. It lists seven principles, including the inherent worth of every person. For 10 points, name this faith.

This Bengali teacher, born Abhay Charan De, founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in New York in 1966. He translated the Bhagavad Gita with commentary. For 10 points, name this swami.
This American organization, led by Elijah Muhammad, taught that Wallace Fard Muhammad was Allah in person. Malcolm X was one of its ministers before leaving in 1964. For 10 points, name this group.

This New York farmer predicted that Christ would return in 1843 or 1844. His calculation drew on the 2300 days in the Book of Daniel. His followers, called by his surname, experienced the Great Disappointment. For 10 points, name this man.

This Jamaican activist founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association and promoted "Back to Africa." Rastafari revere him as a prophet. He founded the Black Star Line and was deported from the United States in 1927 after a mail fraud conviction. For 10 points, name this man.

q: This enzyme complex's alpha and beta subunits spin a central gamma stalk as protons flow through its membrane-embedded Fo portion. Paul Boyer proposed a binding change mechanism for it, and John Walker determined its structure. It is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and thylakoid membrane. For 10 points, name this enzyme that makes the main energy currency of the cell from ADP and phosphate.

These cellular structures are made of ribosomal RNA and proteins in large and small subunits, and the 80S version is found in eukaryotes. The peptidyl transferase activity is carried out by the rRNA, making them ribozymes. They have A, P, and E sites for tRNA. For 10 points, name these organelles where translation occurs.

Barbara McClintock discovered these mobile genetic elements in maize, noting that they caused variegated kernel colors by moving between positions in the genome. Class I types move through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase, while class II types use a cut-and-paste mechanism with transposase. She received a Nobel Prize in 1983 for this work. For 10 points, name these "jumping genes."

This process in eukaryotes occurs in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase II synthesizes pre-mRNA. Introns are removed by the spliceosome after it. A TATA box in the promoter is recognized by general initiation factors before it starts. For 10 points, name this process by which a DNA sequence is copied into messenger RNA.

Meselson and Stahl showed that DNA replication has this property by growing bacteria on nitrogen-15 and then nitrogen-14 and examining bands in a cesium chloride gradient. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density. Each new double helix contains one old strand and one new strand. For 10 points, name this model of replication, as opposed to conservative or dispersive.

This organelle has a double membrane with folds called cristae and contains its own circular DNA. It is the site of the Krebs cycle and most ATP production in eukaryotic cells. Lynn Margulis popularized the endosymbiotic theory for its origin. For 10 points, name this "powerhouse of the cell."

This hormone from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol. It is cleaved from pro-opiomelanocortin along with beta-endorphin. Its release is stimulated by corticotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus. For 10 points, name this hormone abbreviated ACTH.

The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele frequencies stay constant in the absence of mutation, gene flow, genetic drift, natural selection, and non-random this activity. The principle's equation is p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. For 10 points, name this activity, which in Hardy-Weinberg must be random, referring to choosing partners.

This process of cell division produces four genetically distinct haploid cells and includes crossing over in prophase I. It is used to make gametes in animals. Its two successive divisions are called I and II, and the first one reduces the chromosome number. For 10 points, name this type of division, distinct from mitosis, though its name looks similar.

This molecule has a cloverleaf secondary structure and carries an amino acid on its 3-prime end, with an anticodon loop that pairs with mRNA. Aminoacyl synthetases charge it. It was first described by Robert Holley, who sequenced one for alanine. For 10 points, name this adapter in translation, abbreviated tRNA.

This signaling molecule's cyclic form, abbreviated cAMP, was discovered by Earl Sutherland as a second messenger. It is produced from ATP by adenylyl cyclase after a G protein-coupled receptor is activated. For 10 points, name this second messenger that activates protein kinase A.

This 1952 experiment used bacteriophages labeled with radioactive sulfur and phosphorus to show that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material. It was carried out by two researchers at Cold Spring Harbor. For 10 points, name this experiment named for its two scientists, with a blender.

This type of bond holds the two strands of DNA together, joining adenine to thymine with two of them and guanine to cytosine with three. They are weak individually but strong in number. For 10 points, name this bond, which also holds water molecules together.

These cells in the immune system produce antibodies after maturing from B cells. They have an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum, enabling high protein secretion. For 10 points, name these cells whose name refers to the fluid part of blood plus the term for cell.

This disease is caused by a single glutamic acid to valine substitution in the beta chain of hemoglobin. Heterozygous carriers have resistance to malaria, an example of heterozygote advantage. Deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes, deforming red blood cells. For 10 points, name this genetic disease with a crescent-shaped cell.

This enzyme, discovered in thermophilic bacteria from Yellowstone, is used in PCR because it survives denaturation temperatures. Kary Mullis developed the technique that uses it. For 10 points, name this heat-stable DNA polymerase, whose name comes from Thermus aquaticus.

This organ of the human body filters blood to produce urine, using functional units called nephrons. Humans typically have two of them, located near the lower back. For 10 points, name this organ whose failure requires dialysis.

This man proposed a system of binomial nomenclature in his Systema Naturae, giving each species a genus and species name. He is called the father of taxonomy. For 10 points, name this Swedish botanist, whose name is often Latinized as Linnaeus.

This phase of the cell cycle contains the restriction point, where cells commit to division, and is regulated by the retinoblastoma protein and cyclin D. Cells that exit the cycle enter a resting state, G zero, from it. For 10 points, name this first gap phase, preceding S phase.

These biomolecules are polymers of amino acids and fold into primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structures. Alpha helices and beta sheets are examples of secondary structure in them. Enzymes are mostly these. For 10 points, name this class of macromolecule.

This is the process by which water vapor leaves the stomata of plants. It creates a pull that draws water up the xylem from the roots. For 10 points, name this plant process whose name combines "trans" and a word for breathing out.

This Danish physician developed a stain that distinguishes bacteria by cell wall structure, resulting in purple and pink cells. Gram-positive bacteria retain crystal violet because of thick peptidoglycan. For 10 points, name this man whose name is attached to the stain.

This type of natural selection favors both extreme phenotypes over the intermediate one, which can lead to a bimodal distribution. It differs from stabilizing and directional selection. For 10 points, name this type of selection, whose name suggests a rupture.

This molecule is the final electron acceptor in the aerobic electron transport chain, forming water at cytochrome c oxidase. Its absence slows oxidative phosphorylation. For 10 points, name this gas, which humans breathe in.
This group of plants, which includes pines and firs, bear seeds in cones and have needle-like leaves. They are gymnosperms. For 10 points, name this group named for their cone-bearing habit.

This protein, a tumor suppressor sometimes called the "guardian of the genome," halts the cell cycle after DNA damage, and is mutated in about half of all cancers. Li-Fraumeni syndrome arises from a germline mutation of its gene. For 10 points, name this protein named for its molecular weight in kilodaltons.

This process in bacteria transfers DNA through a pilus from a donor with an F plasmid to a recipient. It is one of three ways that bacteria exchange genetic material along with transformation and transduction. For 10 points, name this process, a bacterial analogue of mating.

This is the basic unit of heredity, a segment of DNA that codes for a protein or functional RNA. Mendel called it a factor, and Wilhelm Johannsen coined the modern word. Alleles are alternative versions of it. For 10 points, name this unit located at a specific locus on a chromosome.

This neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction and binds nicotinic receptors on muscle cells. Its breakdown is by acetylcholinesterase, and it is blocked by curare. For 10 points, name this neurotransmitter with an abbreviation ACh.

This cycle in the mitochondrial matrix begins when acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate, catalyzed by citrate synthase. It produces NADH, FADH2, and GTP while releasing two carbon dioxide molecules per turn. Hans Krebs described it in 1937. For 10 points, name this cycle, also called the citric acid cycle.

parts: What organelle contains chlorophyll?
What organelle modifies and packages proteins, with a stack of flattened cisternae named for an Italian biologist?
What protein, discovered by Peter Agre, forms water channels in cell membranes?

q: Answer these questions about genetics.
parts: What type of cell division produces two identical daughter cells?
What term describes an organism's observable traits, as opposed to its genetic makeup?
What type of chromosomal change involves an extra copy of chromosome 21 causing Down syndrome?

q: Answer these questions about the human body.
parts: What pigment in red blood cells carries oxygen?
What hormone from the pancreas lowers blood glucose?
What part of the brain, found at the back and below the cerebrum, coordinates movement and balance?

q: Answer these questions about evolution.
parts: What kind of selection is the process by which organisms better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more?
What group of finches on the Galapagos Islands helped inspire Darwin's thinking?
What term describes similar structures in different species arising from separate evolutionary origins, like wings of bats and insects?

q: Answer these questions about plants.
parts: What pigment makes plants green?
What waxy outer layer on leaves reduces water loss?
What class of plant hormones, first found in a fungus that makes rice seedlings grow tall, promotes stem elongation?

q: Answer these questions about microbiology.
parts: What type of microorganism, of the genus Saccharomyces, is used in baking and brewing?
What Hungarian physician advocated handwashing to prevent childbed fever?
What German physician identified the bacterium causing tuberculosis and gave his name to postulates for linking microbes to disease?

q: Answer these questions about molecular biology.
parts: What term describes the three-nucleotide sequence coding for an amino acid?
What molecule carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes?
What enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix at the replication fork?

q: Answer these questions about ecology.
parts: What term describes the green leaf pores that open and close to exchange gases?
What term describes the relationship in which both species benefit?
What term describes the maximum population an environment can support?

q: This process converts atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia over an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure, roughly 200 atmospheres. Carl Bosch scaled it up industrially at BASF. It made synthetic fertilizers possible and also supplied explosives for World War I. For 10 points, name this process developed by a German chemist who won the 1918 Nobel Prize.

This rule predicts that when hydrogen bromide adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen attaches to the carbon that already bears more hydrogens. It is explained by the greater stability of the more substituted carbocation. A Russian chemist from Kazan proposed it in 1869. For 10 points, name this regioselectivity rule.

These elements, with atomic numbers 57 through 71, fill the 4f subshell and are usually shown in a detached row beneath the main periodic table. They have very similar chemical properties, which made them hard to separate, and cerium is the most abundant of them. Many are used in strong magnets and phosphors. For 10 points, name this series of rare-earth elements that begins with lanthanum.

In this type of reaction, an electron pair is donated by a nucleophile to a carbon bearing a leaving group. The first, called SN1, goes through a carbocation, while the second, SN2, is concerted with inversion of configuration. For 10 points, name this reaction type, abbreviated with an S and a N.

This is the most abundant element in the universe and the lightest element, with an atomic number of one. Its most common isotope has no neutron. It makes up most of the mass of the Sun. For 10 points, name this element with symbol H.

These elements, found in group 18, have filled valence shells and are therefore largely unreactive. Neil Bartlett made the first compound of one with platinum hexafluoride. For 10 points, name this group, including helium, neon, and argon.

This quantum number, symbolized l, determines the shape of an orbital, with s, p, d, and f corresponding to values 0 through 3. It is also called the azimuthal quantum number. For 10 points, name this quantum number, named for the angular momentum of the electron.

This equation, PV equals nRT, relates pressure, volume, amount, and temperature for a hypothetical type of gas that has no intermolecular forces. For 10 points, name this equation of state, for a "perfect" kind of gas.
This type of bond involves the sharing of electron pairs between two atoms, as in the molecule of water. It typically forms between nonmetals. For 10 points, name this bond, distinct from ionic.

This law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of the pathway, as long as initial and final conditions are the same. It is named for a Swiss-born Russian chemist. For 10 points, name this law for adding enthalpies.

This reaction between a conjugated diene and a dienophile forms a six-membered ring in a concerted pericyclic process. Otto Diels and Kurt Alder shared the 1950 Nobel Prize for it. For 10 points, name this cycloaddition reaction.

In this process, an electrolyte solution undergoes a nonspontaneous reaction when current is passed through it. Michael Faraday formulated laws for it, and it is used to produce aluminum and chlorine. For 10 points, name this process, a use of electrical energy to drive chemistry.

This acid, with formula HCl, is found in the human stomach and is also used for cleaning metal. It is a strong acid that dissociates completely in water. For 10 points, name this acid, with a name referring to a chlorine-containing hydrogen compound.

This scientist's model of the atom, proposed in 1913, has electrons in quantized circular orbits and explains the spectrum of hydrogen. He later headed an institute in Copenhagen and won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His principle of complementarity was debated with Einstein. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist.

This equation relates the rate constant of a reaction to temperature as k equals A times e to the negative E a over R T. It shows that rates increase exponentially with temperature. For 10 points, name this equation from a Swedish chemist.

These are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and so different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are examples, and the latter is used in radiocarbon dating. Hydrogen has three common ones, including deuterium and tritium. For 10 points, name this term.
This is the term for the minimum energy required for a reaction to proceed, represented by the height of the barrier on an energy diagram. Catalysts lower it. For 10 points, name this energy.

This rule says that electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing up. For example, in a p subshell, three electrons occupy three different orbitals. For 10 points, name this rule named for a German physicist.

This type of isomerism occurs when two molecules are non-superimposable mirror images, as in L and D amino acids. A carbon with four different groups is called a center of this. For 10 points, name this property of "handedness."

This scale, from zero to fourteen, uses the concentration of hydronium ions to measure acidity; solutions below seven are acids. For 10 points, name the quantity that equals the negative log of hydrogen ion concentration.

This family of organic compounds contains a carbonyl group bonded to a hydrogen and an R group, as in formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. They are oxidized to carboxylic acids. For 10 points, name this functional group.

This law relates the absorbance of light by a solution to its concentration, the path length, and a molar absorptivity. Spectrophotometers rely on it to find concentrations from a calibration curve. It is named for a German physicist and for a Swiss-German mathematician, joined by a hyphen. For 10 points, name this absorbance law.

This is the process of a solid changing directly into a gas without passing through the liquid phase. Dry ice does this at room temperature and ordinary pressure, as does iodine when heated gently. Its reverse is called deposition. For 10 points, name this phase change.

This element has atomic number 79 and symbol Au, from the Latin aurum. It is dense, malleable, and unreactive, dissolving only in aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids. Rutherford's famous scattering experiment used foil made of it. For 10 points, name this precious metal.

This law states that the pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of each component. It is named for an English chemist who also proposed an atomic theory. For 10 points, name this law named for a man who also studied color blindness.
This is the term for a substance, often a metal such as platinum, that speeds up a reaction without being consumed. Enzymes act as biological examples. For 10 points, name this term.

This element, with atomic number 8, is necessary for combustion and respiration. It makes up about a fifth of Earth's atmosphere, and its allotrope ozone forms a protective layer high above. Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele both isolated it. For 10 points, name this element with symbol O.

This family of organic compounds has a hydroxyl group bonded to a saturated carbon. The simplest, with one carbon, is methanol. For 10 points, name this functional group, such as ethanol in beverages.
This principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers. It was formulated by an Austrian physicist. For 10 points, name this principle.

This type of compound consists of a central metal atom or ion bound to surrounding ligands, as in cisplatin and the heme group. Alfred Werner won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining their structure. For 10 points, name this class of compounds with a central metal atom and attached ligands.
Answer these questions about the periodic table.
parts: What is the most electronegative element, with symbol F?
What group of elements includes sodium and potassium and reacts vigorously with water?
What Russian chemist arranged elements by atomic weight in 1869?

q: Answer these questions about acids and bases.
parts: What type of paper turns red in acid and blue in base?
What scientist defined acids as proton donors, alongside a Danish counterpart?
What term describes the product of a neutralization reaction, along with water?

q: Answer these questions about organic chemistry.
parts: What is the simplest alkane, with one carbon?
What term describes hydrocarbons containing one or more carbon-carbon double bonds?
What name is given to the six-carbon aromatic ring proposed by Kekulé?

q: Answer these questions about gas laws.
parts: What scientist's law relates the volume of a gas inversely to its pressure at constant temperature?
What French chemist's law relates volume to temperature at constant pressure?
What term describes a gas that deviates from ideal behavior at high pressure, studied by a Dutch physicist?

q: Answer these questions about chemical bonding.
parts: What kind of bond results from the transfer of electrons from a metal to a nonmetal?
What theory predicts molecular shapes by electron pair repulsion, abbreviated VSEPR?
What is the hybridization of carbon in ethylene?

q: Answer these questions about thermodynamics.
parts: What term describes a reaction that releases heat?
What quantity, symbolized S, measures disorder?
What quantity, symbolized G and named for a Yale scientist, determines reaction spontaneity?

q: Answer these questions about laboratory techniques.
parts: What lab glassware is used for precise measurement of liquid volume during a titration, with a stopcock?
What separation technique uses a mobile phase and a stationary phase, for example on paper?
What technique measures mass-to-charge ratios of ions, abbreviated MS?

q: Answer these questions about kinetics and equilibrium.
parts: What term describes the speed at which reactants are consumed?
What is the term for the expression of products over reactants at equilibrium, symbolized K?
What term describes the slowest step in a mechanism?

q: Answer these questions about famous chemists.
parts: Which French chemist is called the father of modern chemistry and was guillotined in 1794?
Which New Zealand-born physicist proposed the nuclear model of the atom after his gold foil experiment?
Which American chemist won Nobel Prizes in both Chemistry and Peace, and wrote about the nature of the chemical bond?

q: This effect, explained by Einstein in 1905, occurs when light of sufficiently high frequency ejects electrons from a metal surface. The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency but not intensity. Below a threshold frequency, no electrons are emitted regardless of brightness. For 10 points, name this effect that supports the particle nature of light.

This quantity for a rotating body equals the product of its moment of inertia and its angular velocity. It is conserved when no net external torque acts, which is why a spinning figure skater speeds up when pulling in her arms. Kepler's second law reflects its conservation. For 10 points, name this rotational analogue of linear momentum.

This law states that the induced electromotive force in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through it. It underlies electric generators and transformers. For 10 points, name this law of electromagnetic induction named for an English scientist.

This experiment, performed in 1887 by Albert Michelson and Edward Morley, attempted to detect the motion of Earth through a hypothetical medium for light. It found no difference in the speed of light with direction. For 10 points, name the medium that this experiment failed to detect, a "luminiferous" substance.

This is the SI unit of electrical resistance, equal to one volt per ampere. It is symbolized by the Greek letter omega. For 10 points, name this unit named for a German physicist who formulated a law relating voltage, current, and resistance.

This principle says that the buoyant force on an object immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. It explains why steel ships can float and was supposedly discovered in a bathtub. For 10 points, name this principle named for a Greek scientist of Syracuse.

This phenomenon occurs when waves bend as they pass around obstacles or through openings comparable in size to their wavelength. It produces the patterns seen in single slit experiments and in X-ray crystallography. For 10 points, name this phenomenon that distinguishes waves from particles in classical physics.

This type of wave has particles vibrating perpendicular to the direction of travel, like waves on a rope. Light is an example. For 10 points, name this wave type contrasted with longitudinal waves such as sound.

This equation, discovered by a Scottish physicist in the 1860s, is actually a set of four equations unifying electricity, magnetism, and light. It predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. For 10 points, name these equations named for James Clerk Maxwell.

This principle states that along a streamline in steady flow of an ideal fluid, an increase in speed comes with a decrease in pressure. It is used to explain the operation of a Venturi tube and the lift on a wing. It was published in Hydrodynamica by a member of a Swiss family of mathematicians. For 10 points, name this principle.

This is the term for the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another, described by Snell's law. It explains why a straw looks bent in a glass of water and why a pool seems shallower than it is. It occurs because light changes speed. For 10 points, name this phenomenon.

This physicist's equation, a partial differential equation, describes how the quantum state of a system changes with time, with the Hamiltonian operator. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Paul Dirac. For 10 points, name this Austrian physicist who also proposed a cat thought experiment.

This number, equal to the ratio of speed of light in vacuum to the speed in a medium, is always at least one. Water has a value of about 1.33. For 10 points, name this number that determines how much light bends.

This is the force that a stretched or compressed object exerts to return to its shape, described by Hooke's law. It is proportional to displacement. For 10 points, name this force exerted by a coil on a toy slinky, or one that bounces a car.

This particle, discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932, has the same mass as an electron but opposite charge. Dirac's equation predicted its existence. When it meets an electron, both are annihilated into gamma rays. For 10 points, name this antimatter counterpart of the electron.

This phenomenon causes the observed frequency of a wave to differ from the emitted frequency when the source and observer are in relative motion. It explains the change in pitch of a passing siren. For 10 points, name this effect named for an Austrian physicist.
